name: Chinati Foundation
overview: Contemporary art museum in Marfa, Texas, based on the ideas of the artist Donald Judd, preserving and presenting permanent large-scale installations by a limited number of artists (Wikipedia).

Judd first visited Marfa in 1971 and moved there full time in 1977. Construction began in 1979 with initial assistance from the Dia Art Foundation in New York, and the museum opened to the public in 1986 (Wikipedia).
The foundation occupies 340 acres on the former site of Fort D. A. Russell, plus buildings in downtown Marfa, at 1 Cavalry Row (Wikipedia).
funding_verdict: Chinati Foundation: private philanthropy: foundations and individual donors, with Dia's early support

name: Fallingwater
overview: House museum at 1491 Mill Run Road in Mill Run, Fayette County, in the Laurel Highlands, about 70 miles southeast of Pittsburgh (fallingwater.org).

Edgar J. Kaufmann Sr., owner of a Pittsburgh department store, and Liliane Kaufmann commissioned Frank Lloyd Wright. The design dates from 1935 and the main house, guest house and service wing were finished in 1939. Their son Edgar Kaufmann jr. gave the house and 469 acres to the Western Pennsylvania Conservancy in 1963, and public tours began in 1964 (fallingwater.org).
The sources read do not say how the house got its name, and no earlier name was found.
funding_verdict: Fallingwater: private non-profit: Conservancy members, donors and tickets, with a state grant for the three-year repair finished in 2026

press_items.title: Josh Niland, "Frank Lloyd Wright's Fallingwater completes years-long renovation" (2026)
Kaitlyn Hughes, "What's Going On With Fallingwater?" (2025)

name: ABC No Rio
overview: Volunteer-led, collectively run arts and activism centre at 156 Rivington Street on the Lower East Side of Manhattan. Its site calls it a "nonprofit community center for arts and activism" operating since 1980.

Grew out of The Real Estate Show, organised by the artists' group Colab in late 1979 in an abandoned building at 123 Delancey Street. City officials closed the show within a day, and the organisers then negotiated the use of 156 Rivington Street (Wikipedia).
Named after a partly burnt neon sign that once read "Abogado Con Notario". Only fragments remained (Wikipedia).
funding_verdict: ABC No Rio: mainly public capital funding for the new building, plus donations and benefit income

press_items.title: Kevin Erickson, "Reclaiming New York for Local Arts: ABC No Rio" (10 January 2008)

name: Alice Austen House
overview: Museum in the photographer's former home at 2 Hylan Boulevard on the Staten Island shore, in Alice Austen Park near the Verrazano-Narrows Bridge (aliceausten.org).

Built in the 1690s or early 1700s as a one-room Dutch Colonial house. Austen's grandfather John Haggerty Austen bought, renamed and remodelled it in 1844. Preservationists led by Berenice Abbott and Philip Johnson saved it from demolition in the 1950s and 1960s. New York City bought it in 1975 and it opened as a museum in 1985 (English Wikipedia).
Named for Alice Austen (1866 to 1952), who took more than 7,000 photographs (aliceausten.org). The sources read do not give the name her grandfather chose.
funding_verdict: Alice Austen House: mixed public and foundation money: NYC owns the house, a non-profit runs it on city, state and federal grants and foundations

press_items.title: Cynthia Laird, "Why don't more people know about Alice Austen?" (2021)
Coen Projekts (Nadia Coen), "The Alice Austen House Museum" (2019)

name: Apexart
overview: Non-profit exhibition space at 291 Church Street in Tribeca, Lower Manhattan, that picks most of its shows by open call, in which jurors do not see the submitters' names (Wikipedia; apexart website).

Founded in 1994 by Steven Rand, who also directs it (Wikipedia). The tax filing is under the name Apex Art Curatorial Program Inc, a 501(c)(3) exempt since April 1998, with Rand listed as president and executive director (ProPublica).

Brooklyn Rail (Darragh McNicholas, September 2014) reports Rand living above the gallery and credits apexart with more than 170 exhibitions featuring over 1,500 artists, four books of essays and a residency programme.
funding_verdict: apexart: mainly private giving plus public arts grants: foundations, national, state and city arts agencies, and foreign cultural bodies

press_items.title: Darragh McNicholas, "Twenty Years of apexart: A Profile of Founder Steven Rand" (2014)

name: CUE Art Foundation
overview: Non-profit gallery and artist programme at 137 West 25th Street, ground floor, between 6th and 7th Avenues, in Chelsea, Manhattan (CUE website).

Established in 2003. The idea came after 9/11 from shipping executive Thomas K. Y. Hsu, with painter Gregory Amenoff as co-founder and titular head. Its name is a play on "curate" (Brooklyn Rail, April 2021).
Its first gallery was at 511 West 25th Street. In 2012 rising Chelsea rents moved it to the current storefront, which an anonymous donor bought and renovated (Brooklyn Rail).
funding_verdict: CUE Art Foundation: mainly private philanthropy: foundation grants, individual members and donors, with federal arts money

name: Center for Cuban Studies
overview: Non-profit educational institution at 20 Jay Street, Suite 301, Brooklyn, which runs the Cuban Art Space gallery (the Center's site).
Founded in 1972 according to the Center, and co-founded by Sandra Levinson with Saul Landau and Lee Lockwood (Wikipedia). Levinson is executive director.
Its stated purpose is to counter the effects of US policy toward Cuba, including an end to the embargo (the Center).
funding_verdict: Center for Cuban Studies: donations plus program fees and sales of art and merchandise; contributions were 65.6 to 80.5 percent of revenue in 2020 to 2024

press_items.title: Yanelis Abreu, "Art with Afro-Cuban roots in New York" (2013)

name: Modulightor Building (Paul Rudolph Institute)
overview: Building at 246 East 58th Street, between Second and Third Avenues in Manhattan's midtown design district. The Institute holds its office, an exhibit space, the Modulightor showroom and the Rudolph-designed duplex there (Institute).

Paul Rudolph and his partner Ernst Wagner bought the site in February 1989. The first four floors went up from 1989 to 1992. Two more floors and a roof deck were added later by architect Mark Squeo, dated 2007 to 2015 by the Institute and 2010 to 2016 by Curbed. The exterior became a New York City Landmark on 19 December 2023 and the duplex an Interior Landmark on 6 May 2025 (Institute, Curbed).
Named for Modulightor, the lighting company Rudolph founded in 1976 and made Wagner its director (Institute).
funding_verdict: Modulightor Building (Paul Rudolph Institute): private non-profit: the founder's gift of the building and company, plus tickets, memberships and donations

press_items.title: Anthony Paletta, "A Paul Rudolph on 58th Street That Will Actually Last" (2026)

name: Printed Matter, Inc.
overview: Non-profit art bookstore and publisher of artists' books at 231 Eleventh Avenue in Chelsea, New York, its location since 2015 (Wikipedia).

Founded in 1976 in Tribeca by a loose consortium of artists, critics and publishers including Sol LeWitt, Lucy Lippard, Edit DeAk, Pat Steir, Walter Robinson and Carl Andre (Wikipedia). It began as a for-profit art space and had 501(c)(3) non-profit status by 1978 (Wikipedia).
Ingrid Sischy was the first director in 1976. AA Bronson was executive director from 2004 to 2010 and started the New York Art Book Fair in 2006 (Wikipedia).
funding_verdict: Printed Matter, Inc.: grant-funded: private foundations and public arts agencies, plus board and supporter giving
wider_context: DNAinfo (Maya Rajamani, "'We Failed' To Design Park That Benefited Neighbors, High Line Creator Says", 13 February 2017) reported High Line co-founder Robert Hammond telling CityLab "Ultimately, we failed", and that the park has been accused of putting gentrification into "hyperdrive." The article does not name Phil Aarons or Printed Matter.

W Magazine (Jim Lewis, 26 August 2014) describes Aarons as one of the first advisers to the High Line and as president of the Printed Matter board, and the Los Angeles Art Book Fair 2023 site lists Phil Aarons and Shelley Fox Aarons among its lead supporters.

press_items.title: Matt Stromberg, "Printed Matter Window Display Divides Audiences on Israel-Palestine" (25 July 2024)

name: Recess
overview: Non-profit arts organisation at 46 Washington Avenue, Brooklyn, its address since 2018 (Recess website).
Allison Freedman Weisberg founded Recess in 2009, opening in SoHo, Manhattan, at 41 Grand Street. It became the registered non-profit Recess Activities Inc. in 2010 (Recess website).

Session, its artist residency programme, began with its first artist in 2009. Assembly, launched in 2017 at 370 Schermerhorn Street, supports system-impacted youth through art and storytelling. A Critical Writing fellowship began in 2011 (Recess website).
funding_verdict: Recess: grant-funded non-profit: public arts agencies, foundations and individual donors

name: Renee & Chaim Gross Foundation
overview: Historic townhouse and studio of the sculptor Chaim Gross at 526 LaGuardia Place, just south of Washington Square Park in Greenwich Village. The nearest subway stations are Bleecker Street (6) and West 4th Street (A, B, C, D, E, F, M) (foundation's site).

The foundation was first established in 1974 with donations from over two dozen friends and supporters of Gross, was incorporated as a 501(c)(3) in 1989 and opened to the public in 1994. The third floor opened in 2009 (foundation's site).
Named for the sculptor Chaim Gross (1902 to 1991) and his wife Renee. Their children Mimi Gross and Yehudah Gross are its president and vice president (foundation's site, English Wikipedia).
funding_verdict: Renee & Chaim Gross Foundation: small private foundation: donations plus New York State and preservation grants

name: SculptureCenter
overview: Non-collecting contemporary art museum at 44-19 Purves Street, Long Island City, Queens (sculpture-center.org, Wikipedia).

Founded in 1928 by the sculptor Dorothea H. Denslow as The Clay Club in Crown Heights, Brooklyn, first as a studio shared with local children and later other artists. It later moved to the West Village (1932) and to a carriage house on East 69th Street (1948), where it ran an artists' school (Wikipedia).
In 2001 the board closed the school, sold the carriage house for $4.75 million and moved to Queens as a European-style kunsthalle (Wikipedia).
funding_verdict: SculptureCenter: mixed: private foundations and individuals, with New York City and New York State arts money

press_items.title: Seph Rodney, "When the Language Meant to Prop Up Art Makes It Fall Over" (2017)
Benjamin Sutton, "An Exhibition of Sea Creatures and Beach Gear Treads Water" (2016)

name: Storefront for Art and Architecture
overview: Independent non-profit gallery for art and architecture at 97 Kenmare Street in SoHo, Manhattan (Wikipedia, storefront.nyc).
Founded in 1982 by Kyong Park, R.L. Seltman and Arleen Schloss in a small storefront at 51 Prince Street. It moved to Kenmare Street in 1986 (Wikipedia).

Directors: Kyong Park (executive director 1982 to 1998), Sarah Herda, Joseph Grima, Eva Franch i Gilabert (2010 to 2018) and José Esparza Chong Cuy (2018 to the present) (Wikipedia). Esparza Chong Cuy signs as Executive Director and Chief Curator (year-end letter, December 2024).
funding_verdict: Storefront for Art and Architecture: mainly foundations and public arts funds, plus individual donors and members

press_items.title: Patrick McGraw, "Lost & Found: New York's Storefront for Art and Architecture's 40th Birthday" (2022)

name: Swiss Institute
overview: Contemporary art institute at 38 St. Marks Place at Second Avenue in the East Village, Manhattan (Wikipedia).

Founded in 1986 by "a group of Swiss expats looking to highlight their country's artists and culture". The article does not name them (Wikipedia). It began in the Swiss Townhouse at 35 West 67th Street, then moved to 495 Broadway in 1994, 18 Wooster Street from 2011, a temporary space at 102 Franklin Street from 2016, and St. Marks Place from 2018 (Wikipedia).

Building: a former bank of about 700 square metres, redesigned by Selldorf Architects as a four-storey building with exhibition space, an education and public programmes floor, a library and a rooftop. Printed Matter's St. Mark's bookstore occupies the ground floor (Wikipedia).
funding_verdict: Swiss Institute: mixed: private foundations, Swiss and other governments, and New York public arts funds

press_items.title: Hakim Bishara, "Open Letter Asks Swiss Institute to Address Claims Against Artist" (9 October 2019, updated 2021)

name: Triple Canopy
overview: New York nonprofit (501(c)(3)) magazine that publishes digital art and literature, public conversations, exhibitions and books. It is certified by W.A.G.E. (Working Artists and the Greater Economy) and is a member of the Coalition of Small Arts (CoSA) New York (Triple Canopy website).
Founded in 2007 as an "informal, nonhierarchical, geographically dispersed editorial collective". The first issue appeared on 17 March 2008 (Triple Canopy website).

Offices: 264 Canal Street, 3W, New York, NY 10013 since summer 2016. Before that 155 Freeman Street in Greenpoint, Brooklyn, for about five years, and a shared storefront at 177 Livingston Street, Brooklyn, for nine months in 2010 (Triple Canopy website). Wikipedia says the office and venue are in Chinatown, shared with Electronic Arts Intermix.
funding_verdict: Triple Canopy: foundation and public grants: US arts foundations, the National Endowment for the Arts, the New York State Council on the Arts and the New York City Department of Cultural Affairs

name: Bemis Center
overview: Artist residency and contemporary art centre at 724 S. 12th Street in the Old Market Historic District of downtown Omaha, Nebraska.
Founded in 1981 by Jun Kaneko, Tony Hepburn, Lorne Falk and Ree Schonlau as "Alternative Worksite" (stated by the centre).

It was formerly housed in the Bemis Omaha Bag Company Building at 614 South 11th Street, severely damaged in a fire in 1999. In 1984 Schonlau set up a consortium of the City of Omaha, the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development, private and corporate foundations and the Mercer family, who owned the vacant Bemis Bag Building (Wikipedia).
funding_verdict: Bemis Center: grant- and donor-funded: foundations, government arts funders and local donors

name: The Gamble House
overview: House museum at 4 Westmoreland Place in Pasadena, on a knoll above the Arroyo Seco (gamblehouse.org, English Wikipedia).

The house, dated 1908, was built by architects Charles and Henry Greene for David and Mary Gamble of the Procter and Gamble Company. The site calls it the most complete and original example of the Greenes' work (gamblehouse.org). Named for the Gambles.

The Gamble family gave the house to the City of Pasadena in 1966 under a family gift agreement, and it has been open to the public since then. It is owned by the City and operated by The Gamble House Conservancy, a non-profit formed in 2019 (gamblehouse.org, Form 990). USC's School of Architecture ran it before that (English Wikipedia).
funding_verdict: The Gamble House: mixed: a city-owned house run by a non-profit on endowment income, gifts and tour revenue

name: Institute of Contemporary Art Philadelphia (ICA)
aliases: ICA at the University of Pennsylvania
Institute of Contemporary Art, University of Pennsylvania
overview: A contemporary art institute at 118 S. 36th Street, Philadelphia, on the University of Pennsylvania campus (museum website).
Founded in 1963, and the museum describes itself as a non-collecting institution that develops and presents exhibitions, commissions and events (museum website, About).
What is there: no permanent collection; it shows changing exhibitions and publishes books and editions (museum website).
funding_verdict: Institute of Contemporary Art Philadelphia: university-hosted, funded by donors and Penn, with free admission underwritten by a couple

name: Slought
overview: Experimental cultural organisation and 501(c)(3) nonprofit at 4017 Walnut Street in University City, between 40th and 41st streets, next to the Daily Pennsylvanian's offices. It is affiliated with the University of Pennsylvania (Slought; 34th Street Magazine).

Founded in 2002 by Aaron Levy, English professor Al Filreis and Tom Lussenhop of Penn's real estate office, as the first gallery of the Slought Networks programme. The gallery was set to open on 18 October 2002 (Daily Pennsylvanian, 2002). Levy was executive director and chief curator from 2002 to 2022 (Slought).
Private institution separate from Penn, which leased it the space for six years from 2002 (Daily Pennsylvanian, 2002).
funding_verdict: Slought: independent nonprofit: a Pew project grant, a university lease and programme partnerships with Penn

name: Edith Farnsworth House
overview: Glass-and-steel house at 14520 River Road in Plano, Illinois, on a 62-acre parcel along the Fox River, about 58 miles southwest of Chicago (National Trust).

Ludwig Mies van der Rohe designed and built it from 1946 to 1951 as a weekend retreat for Dr. Edith Farnsworth, a Chicago nephrologist. After she sold it in 1972, Peter Palumbo owned it and opened it to the public in May 1997. The National Trust and Landmarks Illinois bought it at auction in 2003 and it opened to visitors in 2004 (National Trust, English Wikipedia).
Called the Farnsworth House until the Trust rededicated it as the Edith Farnsworth House in fall 2021, named for its first owner (National Trust).
funding_verdict: Edith Farnsworth House: private non-profit: National Trust for Historic Preservation, mostly contributions
